meanings.note: With que it is Brazil's most natural everyday way to say I think / do you think.

examples.text: Eu acho que você tá exagerando.

meanings.note: Marks the current moment resulting from an earlier action.

examples.trans: Now she is in a meeting.

examples.text: Agora tenho que resolver umas coisinhas.
examples.trans: Right now I have to sort out a few little things.

meanings.note: Points to the speaker's location or reinforces demonstratives like isso aqui and esse slide aqui.

examples.text: Ela veio aqui olhar um extintor.
examples.trans: She came here to check an extinguisher.

meanings.note: Points to manner or way.

examples.text: A gente não gosta de ser chamada assim.
examples.trans: We do not like to be called that.

meanings.note: In até logo it looks ahead to the next meeting. The phrase is added as the lesson farewell, not quoted from the selected source window.
Modifies a verb to mean well or carefully, as in olhar bem (look closely).

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Everyday adjective in tá bom (okay), boa tarde (good afternoon), and Bom, pessoal (Well, folks).
Everyday informal Brazilian synonym of colocar or pôr.

examples.text: Na hora de botar de novo, impossível.
examples.trans: When it was time to put it back, impossible.

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.
Deixa eu + infinitive is the natural spoken Brazilian frame for let me...

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

examples.trans: Leave your phone on the desk.

meanings.note: Contraction of de + ele.

examples.text: São umas coisas que sobrou dele.
examples.trans: These are some things left over from him.

meanings.note: Indicates the interior of a room or space, often paired with lá or para.
With que, means 'after / once'.

examples.text: Depois que tu estica, é difícil dobrar.
examples.trans: Once you stretch it, it is hard to fold.
We will talk after the meeting.

meanings.note: Used for folding cloth, sheets, or paper.

examples.text: Depois que estica pra dobrar, é difícil.
examples.trans: Once you stretch it to fold it, it is hard.

meanings.note: Masculine cardinal numeral (feminine duas).

examples.trans: She is looking for two bedrooms.

meanings.note: Coordinating conjunction pronounced [i] in natural Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Ela faltou e adiantou o trabalho.
examples.trans: She missed it and got ahead on her work.
There are good and bad numbers.

meanings.note: Third-person masculine singular subject pronoun.
In lençol de elástico, means a fitted sheet with elastic corners.

examples.text: É tipo um lençol de elástico.
examples.trans: It is like a fitted sheet.

meanings.note: Usually contracts with definite articles to no, na, nos, nas.
Regular -er verb for grasping meaning or an explanation.

examples.trans: I don't understand any of this.

meanings.note: Used here for being present at an event. Vou estar keeps estar in the infinitive after the finite form vou.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: Means pulling something out to its full length.

examples.text: Depois que tu estica, fica grande.
examples.trans: Once you stretch it out, it gets big.

meanings.note: Used for machines, systems, and body organs.
Alone as vocative gente! it means folks/guys; with article a gente it means we/us with third-person singular verbs.

examples.text: Você acha que é melhor que a gente?
examples.trans: Do you think you're better than us?
Oh, folks, the meeting ran late.

meanings.note: Unit of sixty minutes or clock time.

examples.text: Vou ficar lá por uma hora.
examples.trans: I'm going to stay there for an hour.

examples.text: Já está na hora da reunião.
examples.trans: It's already time for the meeting.

meanings.note: Plural impossíveis.

examples.text: Na hora de botar de novo, impossível.
examples.trans: When it came time to put it back, impossible.
It is impossible to get there now.

meanings.note: Digestive organ.

examples.text: O intestino também tava sobrando muito.
examples.trans: The intestine was also very much left over.

meanings.note: Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.
Neutral demonstrative pronoun pointing to what was just said or done.
Plural lençóis; lençol de elástico is a fitted sheet.

examples.text: É tipo um lençol de elástico.
examples.trans: It is like a fitted sheet.

meanings.note: Points to a place away from the speaker; lá dentro reinforces inside there.
Marks comparisons (mais que), negated continuation (não ... mais, not anymore), and the farewell até mais.
A married man in relation to his spouse.

examples.text: Como é que tá meu marido?

examples.trans: Your husband is already doing wonderfully.

meanings.note: Introduces a contrast. The informal thanks softens the refusal; it does not accept the invitation.

examples.trans: It’s a meeting, but I’m not going.

meanings.note: Invariable as an adverb before adjectives or participles.

examples.trans: We thought it was kind of extra.
I can leave it half open.

meanings.note: Agrees with its noun as a determiner/adjective; singular muita coisa idiomatically means many things.

examples.trans: They say a lot of things.

meanings.note: Often used adverbially in Brazilian speech (funcionando normal).

examples.text: Um tá lá dentro dele, funcionando normal.
examples.trans: One is in there inside him, working normally.

meanings.note: In the phrase de novo, means 'again'.

examples.text: Na hora de botar de novo, impossível.
examples.trans: When it was time to put it back again, impossible.

meanings.note: A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.
Ubiquitous spoken contraction of não é used to invite agreement.

examples.text: Isso aqui é um gráfico, né?
examples.trans: This here is a chart, right?

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Stands without um for another (outro gráfico), or with os for the others (os outros).
Used for taking transport, grabbing items, or taking an apartment first.

examples.trans: They will grab it ahead of me.
I do not need to take the subway.

meanings.note: Informal reduced para. Before a feminine noun, this Brazilian spelling can also represent a contraction including the article a; the exact meeting is clear from context.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.

meanings.note: Plural rins.

examples.text: Mas isso aqui é um rim?
examples.trans: But is this here a kidney?

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.
Means being extra or remaining unused.

examples.text: São umas coisas que sobrou dele.
examples.trans: These are some things that were left over from him.
The intestine was also left over.

meanings.note: Adds another person or item to what was already stated.

examples.trans: I want you to go in too.
I'm the one who made it too!

meanings.note: Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.

meanings.note: Informal second-person singular possessive, very common in Rio speech.

examples.trans: Your husband is already doing great.

meanings.note: In colloquial Brazilian speech, é tipo means 'it is kind of like'.

examples.text: É tipo um lençol de elástico.
examples.trans: It is like a fitted sheet.

examples.text: Que tipo de música você ouve?
examples.trans: What kind of music do you listen to?

meanings.note: Everyday verb for removing or taking something out.

examples.trans: We took it out during surgery.

examples.text: Você tira o botão de baixo.
examples.trans: You take the button from the bottom.

meanings.note: Informal singular 'you', often paired with third-person verb forms in casual Rio speech.

examples.trans: You keep it in the freezer.

examples.text: Depois que tu estica, fica difícil.
examples.trans: Once you stretch it, it gets hard.

meanings.note: Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?
